content: A multi-country online survey conducted by the World Hepatitis Alliance and Coalition Plus included 210 anonymous participants from 49 countries. Among these participants, 56% were male, and 71% were aged between 26 and 55 years. Additionally, 23% were living with hepatitis C virus (HCV), 21% were former drug injectors, 18% identified as current drug injectors, and 16% were living with HIV. The survey revealed strong support for decentralized and integrated HCV services, as well as task-sharing approaches. The most preferred service locations were community-based sites (44%) and self-testing at a location of choice (35%), compared to hospitals (28%) or primary care clinics (28%). Community-based organization centers were the most popular sites (50%), followed by hospitals (39%) and general practitioners (29%). Among individuals who currently or formerly injected drugs, preferences for testing and treatment at community-based organization sites or drug user support centers were even stronger (50%). The primary reasons for choosing specific testing and treatment locations included proximity to home or work (53–56%), reduced costs (38–40%), and a non-judgmental, stigma-free environment (37–39%). These preferences were even more pronounced among people who inject drugs and those living with HIV. Furthermore, 91% of participants expressed a strong preference for receiving testing and treatment at the same location, citing convenience (34%) and continuity of care from testing to treatment (33%). Peer-driven interviews and focus group discussions conducted by the International Network of People Who Use Drugs (INPUD) across four key populations (gay and bisexual men, male and female sex workers, people who inject drugs, and transgender individuals) highlighted a universal preference for community-based services for HIV, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and HCV. Participants emphasized that community-led services are essential for promoting the health and human rights of marginalized groups and counteracting stigma in traditional healthcare settings. Key advantages of community-led services included improved accessibility, tailored understanding of community health needs, comprehensive care, safe spaces for advocacy, and effective, non-judgmental communication. Effective community-led service models mentioned included drop-in centers, mobile clinics, peer outreach, and one-stop shops. Participants strongly supported offering HCV testing and direct-acting antiviral (DAA) treatment in diverse settings, such as harm reduction services (needle and syringe programs, opioid agonist maintenance therapy clinics, and drop-in centers), general practice, and hospitals. This approach aimed to maximize access and reduce barriers while minimizing loss to follow-up. A rapid qualitative assessment conducted in 2020 across 10 countries explored the values and preferences of potential HCV service users and healthcare workers regarding hepatitis C self-testing (HCVST) and current testing services. Respondents described existing HCV services as inconvenient, with complex processes, long wait times, immediate payment requirements, and insufficient information on accessing tests and treatments. Simplifying processes through decentralization and integration with primary care and harm reduction services, particularly via one-stop shops for same-day testing and treatment, received strong support. However, concerns were raised about potential stigma if HCV services were exclusively targeted at already marginalized populations. Partial decentralization, where only testing is conducted at the community level without guaranteed prompt access to treatment, was deemed ineffective. The systematic review revealed that the impact of fully decentralized and integrated HCV testing and treatment was most significant among people who inject drugs and prisoners—two populations facing substantial barriers to accessing care and high rates of loss to follow-up. The Guideline Development Group concluded that providing HCV services at lower-level facilities integrated with harm reduction services would enhance equity, particularly for marginalized populations. Task-sharing, defined as redistributing tasks from specialists to trained non-specialist healthcare workers, was recommended to expand access to HCV diagnosis, care, and treatment. This approach has been successfully implemented in HIV care and is supported by evidence showing comparable cure rates between specialists and non-specialists across all populations and settings. Task-sharing was particularly effective in improving access for people who inject drugs and prisoners, who are often harder to reach. Participants in various surveys and interviews emphasized the importance of non-judgmental, stigma-free care and the need to sensitize and train healthcare workers. While many respondents supported task-sharing, they noted that it would not improve access unless healthcare workers' attitudes improved. Peer workers and community-led services were highly valued, especially by marginalized populations, for their ability to build trust and engage effectively. Resource considerations highlighted the cost-effectiveness of simplified care models with task-sharing to nurses or non-specialist doctors, which resulted in lower costs and similar or better outcomes. Feasibility studies demonstrated the success of task-sharing in primary care and harm reduction settings, particularly for marginalized populations. Implementation considerations included defining roles and standards of care, providing training and mentorship, establishing regulatory frameworks, and ensuring integrated data systems and cross-training of healthcare providers. In Cambodia, Médecins Sans Frontières implemented a simplified, decentralized HCV care model in rural Battambang province. The project involved voluntary HCV antibody screening through active and passive case finding, with serology testing conducted using rapid diagnostic tests. Health center staff, primarily nurses, were trained to identify signs of advanced liver disease and manage HCV care. This model demonstrated the feasibility of decentralized HCV care in low-resource settings, addressing barriers to access and improving outcomes for rural populations.
